items.title: Iconic Film Character Intro: Leatherface Became a Horror Icon in Less Than 20 Seconds
items.summary: Leatherface is part of the Mount Rushmore of horror movie killers alongside icons like Freddy Krueger, Michael Myers, and Jason Voorhees. It takes a lot to end up in that pantheon, but for him, it was shockingly easy. Even though less than 20 seconds elapse between his first appearance on-screen in 1974’s The Texas Chain Saw Massacre and the end of the scene, his introductory moment instantly cemented him as a legend of the genre. Let’s break down exactly how this scene works, and why it’s so effective, even more than 50 years later. Leatherface Provides the Movie With A Short, Sharp Shock It’s perhaps worth noting at this point that the movies in the Texas Chainsaw Massacre franchise often challenge traditional notions of who is the “villain” in a story. While Leatherface (Gunnar Hansen) is the primary killer in these movies, he is the product of a wildly abusive household and is often simply defending his home from people who he views as intruders. However, whether or not he is the true antagonist of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, he is a tremendously powerful person who is capable of terrifying violence, as is made perfectly clear by his first appearance in the movie. Up to the moment when Leatherface appears (at the end of the movie’s first act), director Tobe Hooper’s magnum opus has treated audiences to a slow boil as Sally Hardesty (Marilyn Burns) and her friends travel first to the graveyard where her grandfather was buried and then to his rural home (which, unbeknownst to them, is next to a farmhouse that is owned by a cannibalistic family of former slaughterhouse workers). While there are plenty of grody, intense moments packed into the first act, they are more surreal than downright scary, forging a sort of gloomy atmosphere. items.title: Horror Film Season is Officially Here as Fantastic Fest 2026 Kicks Off This Week
items.summary: Sure, it still might be blazing hot and sunny in Austin, Texas, but horror season is set to kick off as it always does in the dark, cold, and always rambunctious theaters of Alamo Drafthouse in Austin, Texas, as Fantastic Fest 2026 kicks off this week. As we’ve done in the past, we’ll be on the ground to check out some of the best genre films from across the globe, with a particular interest in spotting which up-and-coming horror films might be the next Obsession or Backrooms to break through to mainstream success. If you’re planning to attend, or simply want to keep tabs from home, here’s a list of some of our most anticipated films screening at this year’s Fantastic Fest, along with quick links to our podcast roundup from last year’s festivities. Fantastic Fest 2026 Preview It really can’t be overstated just how bonkers the horror filmmaking industry has become over the past few years. For those who have been horror fans or filmmakers for years or decades, it might not be a surprise that films like Obsession and Backrooms broke through to huge box office and cultural success. But for those seeing the darkness for the first time, Fantastic Fest is one of the best film festivals to dive deep into genre filmmaking at its finest. In our coverage last year, we explored why the festival's 20-year anniversary was one of the most important ever for horror filmmakers, with notable titles like Primate, Black Phone 2, and Shelby Oaks among the big headlines. If you missed our coverage last year, you can check out our wrap-up podcast here. This year looks to be just as intriguing and inspiring, with a solid mix of major premieres and up-and-coming horror indies, which we’re excited to cover and explore over the next week. So check out some of our top picks below, and stay tuned for more coverage to come. items.title: The 1954 Samurai Classic That Inspired So Many Other Movies
items.summary: I find that Akira Kurosawa's Seven Samurai (Shichinin no Samurai) is one of those movies you hear about and hear about and then skip because you think it might be pretentious. Then you finally sit down one day and watch it... ...and your life changes forever. That's because this movie rocks. It has action, drama, and beautiful cinematography, and it remains gripping throughout its 3.5-hour runtime. I can't really say enough about how special a movie it is and also how it became the blueprint for modern ensemble cinema. Kurosawa pioneered tropes we take for granted today, like the assembling-the-team montage, the stoic expert leader, training the inexperienced villagers, and multi-camera telephoto action sequences. Today, I want to look at all the movies that were directly influenced by or remade this 1954 classic and discuss how its influence has spread throughout the entire man-on-a-mission genre. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com Direct Remakes & Western Adaptations These are movies that just took the plot of Seven Samurai and made it their own. It's called pastiche or homage, and I think the best writers steal! The Magnificent Seven (1960 & 2016): The most famous direct beat-for-beat translation; it's basically the same movie in the Old West. Ah, and there are no swords. John Sturges traded ronin in feudal Japan for gunfighters and gave us an iconic Elmer Bernstein score plus stars like Yul Brynner and Steve McQueen. The remake with Chris Pratt and Denzel Washington is fun, but nothing beats the original. Battle Beyond the Stars (1980): This was a low-budget affair produced by Roger Corman. His cult sci-fi flick takes the plot into outer space, where a young farmer travels the galaxy recruiting mercenary warriors to save his planet from an evil tyrant. This was more of his Star Wars, which we will get to later. A Bug’s Life (1998): I think about this version all the time, as I like playing it for my son. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The 1957 Glenn Ford Western Line About Time That Still Hits Hard
items.summary: 1957's 3:10 to Yuma was directed by Delmer Daves from a screenplay by Halsted Welles, which itself was based on Elmore Leonard's 1953 short story "Three-Ten to Yuma." Iconic screen star Glenn Ford plays outlaw Ben Wade, with Van Heflin as the rancher Dan Evans. In the Western film, the drought-stricken rancher captures Ben Wade and agrees to hold him in a Contention City hotel until the 3:10 train arrives to take him to prison in Yuma. Partway through their fairly calm standoff, Wade watches and observes something about Evans that feels like a taunt at first but betrays his inner calm. It's one of the great examples of a villain (even an anti-villain) accidentally becoming philosophical and a moment of insight from an unexpected character. Watch the scene below. The Scene The whole film has narrowed to a hotel room, nearly at the climax of the story. Wade's gang is riding toward town. The men Evans expected to help him have fallen off one by one. He's alone with Wade, waiting for the train, the tension rising. Evans has a pocket watch in his hand. He keeps checking it, then squeezing it, as the minutes crawl toward 3:10. The physical business is doing most of the acting. Wade watches Evans do this. Then he speaks. "All you gotta do is drop the gun and let me walk out the door." "Wade, listen—" Evans says. "What are you squeezin' the watch for?" "Are you sure that no one would ever know?" "Squeezin' that watch ain't gonna stop time," Wade says with a smile. A shootout ensues minutes later, but Evans manages to drag Wade through the town to the train, making it despite being outnumbered. Wade isn't wrong about the watch. Evans is squeezing it as if he can crack it, maybe to make the minutes move faster. The line is Wade reading Evans precisely, in an almost quiet and nonthreatening way. items.title: The Queer Horror of Summer Camp Slashers
items.summary: Summer might be over, but I can’t stop thinking about summer camp slashers. Horror got a new, deadly locale in these campground-set movies, often in the lead-up to or during an active summer season, before a killer attacks the campers and counselors. I’m most fascinated with the queer horror that this subgenre has unleashed upon us, and pushing me into this deep dive is my recent viewing of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (2026), a modern summer camp slasher that challenges the monsters of the past. Stay close to the bonfire as we explore how the isolation, the bullying, and the hookups in summer camp slashers have been kindling to feed the queer horror flames for years. And brace yourself, there will be spoilers. Welcome to Crystal Lake ‘Friday the 13th’ (1980)Credit: Paramount Pictures No longer was it the suburbs where Michael Myers stalked victims in 1978’s Halloween, the movie that established the slasher formula. Follow the trail markers, and you will find that the blueprint for this horror subgenre was created by the original Friday the 13th (1980). “The idea for the summer camp came from my instinct that we needed a location where young adults would be cut off from all adult help,” the late Victor Miller, screenwriter of F13, said in an interview. Come nightfall, the unlucky group of counselors reopening Camp Crystal Lake either split off to have sex or play a mild game of strip monopoly, until one by one, they are taken out by a mysterious killer, whose identity, I believe, is queer-coded. A Destructive Mother ‘Friday the 13th’ (1980)Credit: Paramount Pictures Some fun trivia I found out is how connected the F13 franchise is with queer horror fans, thanks to the 2013 retrospective documentary, Crystal Lake Memories: The Complete History of Friday the 13th. items.title: The Funniest Movie of the 2020s is Only Available on YouTube
items.summary: In the past few years, we’ve seen many filmmakers innovate in the comedy genre, utilizing wholly original filmmaking techniques and stylized humor. However, one of the most uniquely impressive films we’ve seen from any filmmaker, let alone in the comedy genre, is only available on YouTube. Let’s talk about Conner O’Malley and Danny Scharar’s Rap World. Plot and Production The film follows a friend group of twenty-something burnouts who fight against their party-oriented temptations to do their best to complete a rap album in one night in 2009 in suburban Pennsylvania. The original idea for the film actually came about in 2020 when O’Malley and co-writer Jack Bensinger incorporated old camcorder footage of teens playing Guitar Hero into one of their other projects. In October of 2020, the pair began production on what was originally going to be a series of short-form skits to be uploaded to YouTube. After these skits didn’t turn out the way the team was initially hoping, they shelved the project for six months before re-editing it into a ten-minute short film. Sensing improvement, the team got together, rewrote a new script, and shot over 70 hours of footage over the course of two to three years, subsequently edited by Bensiger. The team utilized rap music figures for help with some of the music, but maintained a sense of improv on set to elicit the more low-quality elements of the songs. Obviously, these ones are the funniest to listen to. The Absolutely Hysterical Humor ‘Rap World’Credit: Conner O’Malley As someone who studies film for a living, I really do my best to avoid speaking in superlatives when it comes to works that I particularly love. However, I must say that the quotable line-to-runtime ratio for Rap World is perhaps the most extraordinary I’ve seen in a comedy film in my entire life.
